https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8x2.text: Figure caption, Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters in France and use tear gas By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor ,Â Hugh Schofield ,Â in Paris ,Â Nick Beake ,Â in Lille Â and Â Mark Lowen ,Â in Marseille Published 9 hours ago Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la RÃ©publique in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers. The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycÃ©es - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day. Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement. In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction. A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed. "Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart." Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added. Image source, Reuters In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time. President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally. Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation. Figure caption, Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements". He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far. There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The protests began in mid-September but have spread to high schools across France There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases. One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability". Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the ChÃ¢teau d'Ãpluches lycÃ©e for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone. On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens. Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired. The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks. Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police Published 1 day ago School protests send shivers down French government's spine Published 4 days ago What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too. Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September. Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and MichÃ¨le, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing. "We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling. Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/AP View image in fullscreen Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/AP Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side over four years of war Dan Sabbagh , Jessica Elgot and Andrew Roth in Kyiv Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.08 EDT First published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv. The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow . Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing St, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump. “Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.” Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph . That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv. “I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … Of course, people will die.” The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place. Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future. The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices. The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham greeted Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid. As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said. Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday. In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister. Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support. The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it. “Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said. Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.” The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish guards in full ceremonial uniform. Musk said that the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump. Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations. “Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.” Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine. “With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer. It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia. Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv. At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread. Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included. Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Andy Burnham Volodymyr Zelenskyy Donald Trump news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation? https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2026/10.text: Daily Kos Community Street Prophets Friday: Písek, part I (photo diary/open thread) by Marko the Werelynx for Street Prophets Community This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication. Friday, October 9, 2026 at 1:07 PM PDT Recommend Story Share: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Save 65 Comments Add Daily Kos to Google Photo: Marko the Werelynx Greetings and welcome to another little chapter of the Werelynx summer vacation saga. This week, yet a gentle bit of summery fluff, caught in the web brought to you by the miracle of JPEG compression. Dozens of photos easy on your eyes and easy on your bandwidth. And it’s all a mere excuse for posting another open thread. As the autumn reaches a colorful crescendo in these parts, I’m here to drag you back to a warm, overcast summer day and take you on a little journey through the streets of a cozy royal town founded in 1243 on the banks of the Otava River. Marko the Werelynx We’d spent the morning gazing at amazing scaly critters and strolling through the fairgrounds set up along the main street of a town called Protivín. After a short drive we parked in the city of Písek. We were ready for lunch. Photo: Marko the Werelynx We walked along the paved paths along the river, across a little, blue, iron girder bridge and onto a little island. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx The restaurant we picked turned out to be a popular one and we squeezed in next to one of the locals who turned out to be very chatty. Of course, getting a word in with our group blathering wasn’t easy, but we did hear a few tales as we ate our lunch. Photo: Marko the Werelynx This little planter box I found along one side of the restaurant contained herbs. Photo: Marko the Werelynx After lunch we crossed the river on another bridge and explored a bit of the historic downtown area. You might think they’re flying the Ukrainian flag upside-down from those battlements, but that’s the flag of the town of Písek Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Notice any cannonballs? Medium-sized balls, one painted gold embedded in the wall of the top floor and one of a more natural tint in the wall almost at the level of the sidewalk. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Hard to miss the cannonballs dotting the building in the next picture. During the Thirty Years War, Písek was repeatedly bombarded and plundered. During one particularly horrific pogrom, the reported number of surviving civilians was recorded as being “20.” Photo: Marko the Werelynx House at the Silver Denari Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx A peek through the bars at the interior of the church Photo: Marko the Werelynx Marko the Werelynx The building that housed the electrical generator (powered by the river) for the royal town of Písek. Currently a museum, that was closed for renovations. Photo: Marko the Werelynx More of the walls of the old castle. Photo: Marko the Werelynx A look through the trees at the oldest standing bridge in the Czech Republic Photo: Marko the Werelynx We’ll get to that bridge eventually. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Info center and entrance to the castle grounds. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx This arch leads to the town’s malting house. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Castle courtyard. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Town of Písek Photo: Marko the Werelynx Neat little groined arcade that led to the entrance of a gold museum. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Now more of a cultural center than a malting house. Photo: Marko the Werelynx Great Square Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Photo: Marko the Werelynx Thanks for stopping by. Next week I’ll hopefully be bringing you part II of my visit to Písek. This is an open thread. Fake accounts. Fake news. You can help stop it. Greece has opened a stand-alone battery energy storage system (BESS) in Larissa, Thessaly, following a joint investment by METLEN and the Karatzis Group of Companies. The facility has a power capacity of 330MW and an energy storage capability of 790MW-hours (MWh). Find out more The inauguration event was attended by senior government officials including Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Minister of Environment and Energy Stavros Papastavrou. Members of the Greek Parliament, regulatory representatives and local authorities were also present. METLEN and the Karatzis Group developed the project through a joint investment vehicle. The Karatzis Group holds a 51% interest while METLEN retains a 49% stake. METLEN took responsibility for the construction, operational management and maintenance, leveraging its experience in energy storage infrastructure. The project is expected to enhance the flexibility and resilience of Greece’s electricity grid, supporting the integration of renewable energy sources. According to the companies, the facility is seen as an important piece of infrastructure for both the national and wider European energy market. Mitsotakis addressed the ceremony, stating that the new facility is “an important step towards building the Greece of the future”. He emphasised its role in strengthening national energy security and competitiveness, and extended congratulations to METLEN and the Karatzis Group for completing the project. METLEN executive chairman Evangelos Mytilineos said: “I am particularly proud that today, here in Thessaly, we are inaugurating Greece’s largest stand-alone energy storage facility in eastern Europe and one of the largest across the European Union. “This project reflects the new reality of the energy system, as storage, alongside grids and interconnections, is essential if we are to use the clean energy we generate with efficiency and provide businesses and consumers with a more reliable and predictable energy supply.” The investment received loan support from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility – NextGenerationEU. The partnership between METLEN and the Karatzis Group was highlighted as a key factor in the timely and effective delivery of the project. In March 2026, the PPC Group and METLEN formed a joint venture to develop BESS projects totalling up to 1.5GW and 3GW-hours across Romania, Bulgaria and Italy. Sign up for our daily news round-up!
